newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavarian fin min sees German tax revenue falling.
newsitem.headline: Bavarian fin min sees German tax revenue falling.

text.p: Bavarian Finance Minister Erwin Huber said on Wednesday unexpectedly low tax revenues this year were making Germany's efforts to qualify for European monetary union "very, very difficult."

Speaking at a tax conference, Huber said a downward correction was likely in the next official tax revenue estimates in May. He blamed a weak economy and the abolition of a wealth tax for low tax collection in January and February.
Bavarian official sees German tax revenue falling
Bavaria, the home state of German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, took in 5.7 percent less tax revenue in the first two months of this year than in the same period in 1996.

Bavarian tax revenues are eight percent behind plan so far this year, although March figures will give a more reliable indication of tax revenue for the rest of the year, Huber, a member of Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU), said.
Bonn was also seeing a negative trend in tax revenue, a development that could undermine efforts to meet the EMU budget deficit target of three percent of GDP, he said.
The declining efficiency of the German tax system is a key reason behind Waigel's plans to cut taxes and abolish tax breaks in a two-stage plan which would take effect by 1999.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet on Tuesday approved a 1998 tax bill to make cuts in corporate and commercial income taxes which would pave the way for big income tax reductions a year later, leaving taxpayers a net 30 billion marks better off.

The coalition and Social Democrats (SPD) are in touch with each other about restarting talks to seek a tax compromise. The opposition party pulled out of negotiations in a recent row over coal subsidies. Failure to put a deal together would condemn the tax reforms to a possible stalemate in parliament, where the SPD controls the Bundesrat upper house.
